answers.answer: They share family a.298.1.1 because SCOPe groups domains by common ancestry and shared structure, not by chain length. The TAL effector family is a tandem-repeat protein. Each repeat is about 33–35 residues and forms a helix–loop–helix hairpin. The repeats stack into a right-handed superhelix that wraps DNA. Each repeat has a hypervariable loop, the repeat-variable diresidue (RVD) at positions 12–13, which contacts a DNA base. The levels are class a (all alpha), then the TAL effector-like fold a.298, then superfamily a.298.1, then this family. Any TAL effector DNA-binding repeat array has the same repeat architecture and very high repeat-to-repeat sequence similarity, so the family assignment is strong. Because the unit repeats, not the whole chain, define the domain, the entries can differ greatly in length. The length differences have several likely sources: (1) The constructs contain different numbers of repeats. A 2kq5-type entry (the NMR dHax3 structure, as I recall) can cover a different repeat array from the crystal structures 3v6p and 4cj9, so the domain is longer or shorter by multiples of about 34 residues. (2) The structures include different amounts of the N- and C-terminal flanking regions, such as the cryptic repeats or the half-repeat. (3) Some regions are disordered or unresolved in the deposited structure, so the SCOPe domain boundary covers only the modeled part. (4) The proteins are different TALEs or designer TALEs from different species (e.g., Xanthomonas, Ralstonia) with different repeat counts. I am confident of the repeat-length logic but less certain of the exact repeat count or construct in each of the three entries. I recall d2kq5a_ and d3v6pa_ as dHax3 or PthXo1-type TALE structures, but I did not check this against the release. These limits apply. A shared family means a shared repeat fold and a common mechanism of DNA recognition. It does not mean shared DNA-target specificity. Specificity comes from the RVD sequence, and that cannot be transferred between family members by SCOPe membership alone. Repeat number and length also should not be used to infer function, affinity, or the modeled superhelical pitch. The superhelix changes conformation between DNA-free and DNA-bound states. Different domain lengths are also a poor basis for picking a family representative or a modeling template. Choose a template by matching repeat count, RVD content, and whether the structure is DNA-bound, and check the actual release entries.
